subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot begin without saying how amazed I am at that hogwash coming from the previous speaker for the New Democratic Party. If any government followed the philosophies of the New Democratic Party, there would be no small business sector. All that would be left in a country run by the socialists would be larger unions and nationalized Crown corporations.
I would first like to congratulate the new Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) on his appointment. I hope he receives the co-operation from his cabinet that his predecessor, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) did, and not as his previous Liberal predecessors. Otherwise he will become a puppet on a string as they were in the past. I sincerely wish him the best of luck in his deliberations with small business because we all look, from these two parties in any event, at the future of small business in a very non-partisan way.
I am pleased to be taking part in this debate regarding the proposed amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act. I am always delighted to speak on matters which deal with the small business sector because small business, as we know it, still know it, or certainly as we knew it, is certainly the backbone of the economy. Unfortunately, with a lack of attention to that sector, that backbone has been eroding.
Small business, as we have said over and over again, is responsible for over 60 per cent of the labour force in this country. It is certainly the largest potential employer, something that governments, generally speaking, are not taking as much advantage of as possible, especially with the unemployment figure reaching a million in this country.
It is unfortunate that this House debates matters involving small business so seldom, when in fact the whole economy revolves around it. It is also unfortunate that more often than not when this House debates matters dealing with small business, it deals with amendments or extensions of old pieces of legislation merely to keep up with the times, rather than with new innovative programs and policies that truly assist the small business sector. This bill, Bill C-17, is one such example of merely amending the Small Businesses Loans Act in such a
Small Businesses Loans Act
way as to keep up with the times. Naturally it will receive all-round support, for it increases the amount of the maximum guaranteed loan from $75,000 to $100,000. As I said, that merely keeps the level of the loan indexed to the current inflation rate.
I recall in 1977 when similar amendments were made to the Small Businesses Loans Act at which time the ceiling went from $50,000 to $75,000 maximum. At that time a number of us recommended that we should be more generous and raise the level to $100,000 instead of going back to this bill on a tri-annual basis. Perhaps a permanent bill incorporating measures keeping up with inflation could be considered, so that we would not have to come back to deal with these band-aid approaches to small business on a regular basis, as we have been doing. In any event, three years ago dealing with these same amendments I said we should not just deal with this vital sector on an ad hoc basis, as we are doing today again but, rather, that we should develop an over-all comprehensive program for small and medium enterprises in Canada.
Over the years that I was a small business spokesman in this House, my colleagues and I proposed a variety of ideas and recommendations to assist and enhance the growth of the small business sector. In fact, my friend, the hon. member for Capilano, was in the process of developing some of those ideas when he was minister of state for small businesses in the last Parliament. Unfortunately, though, as everyone knows, this development of ideas came to an abrupt and sad end when the Liberals and New Democrats defeated a budget which, I must assume, was defeated for a reason which goes far beyond budgetary measures, namely, political power.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
The Liberals could not have defeated the budget because they did not approve of it. I will explain. The Liberals could not have defeated the budget just because they did not approve of the budgetary measures, because why else would the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) have copied to the cent many of those budgetary measures in his minibudget just a week ago tonight? One of the few things that was left out, of course, was a promise that government spending would not increase any faster than the gross national product. Look what the proposal is now, $4 billion. That was a promise.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) promised during the election campaign after our budget defeat that if interest rates rose after the Liberals formed the government, he would resign. What happened? Interest rates have increased by 3 per cent, and he is still here. The only thing 1 can say to those who supported the Liberals on February 18 is that they have been had. If they believe that energy cost increases are going to stay below 18 cents a gallon, they are fooling themselves as well. The government has been fooling the Canadian people. That is what has been happening. The

April 28, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
Liberals did that in 1974 with wage and price controls. They did it again this time with the budget and with energy policy.
Where is that magic blended price or the magic made-in-Canada price? When all the blending comes together, the cost at the gas pump is going to increase by 50 cents or more a gallon, not 18 cents. We were proposing 18 cents a gallon. We proposed, hand-in-hand, energy tax rebates to low income families, to agricultural producers and to the development of the urban transit system. None of this is being proposed by the Liberals now that they are in government.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised that as soon as he formed the government he would let us know what energy costs were going to be. In December of last year he said that in two weeks he would let us know exactly what that made-in-Canada price would be. Two weeks later he said he would let us know as soon as he formed the government. When he formed the government he still did not know. He still does not tell us, and he still keeps the Canadian public in the dark as far as energy costs are concerned. That is why I am saying to those Canadians who supported the Liberals on February 18 that-and I repeat again-they have been had.
In any event, back to Bill C-17-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: A wonderful digression.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
-three years ago this House also increased the eligibility level of a small business under the Small Businesses Loans Act from maximum annual sales of $1 million to $1.5 million. 1 am somewhat surprised that there is no change in this definition as it pertains to this legislation in Bill C-17. Is there something wrong with growth? Does the Minister of State for Small Businesses or the government think there is something wrong with growth? By not raising the level there would appear to be an incentive for small business to stay small rather than to grow.
But perhaps the most important thing which is missing is a provision which would include venture or working capital as part of this legislation because, after all, the majority of businesses which experience financial difficulties experience them because of a lack of working capital. This is something that I proposed very strenuously the last time this bill was amended in 1977. It was considered and rejected for a variety of reasons, but today more than ever, as far as the economic climate in this country is concerned, it is necessary that working capital or venture capital be included in this bill, and I hope the minister will seriously consider including such a provision when it comes before the appropriate standing committee at which time I, along with my colleagues, will be proposing a number of amendments to try to improve this bill.
However, after all is said and done with regard to this bill, it is really interest rates which harm industry the most, the high cost of borrowing money. Members of this government only two or three months ago were saying that they should be elected because they would bring interest rates down. One credit I must give to the government is for copying parts of that John Crosbie budget, and one of the measures in that
budget which the government copied is the small business development bond, but that is not enough.
Three months ago this Liberal administration, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has said over the past few months, knew what was wrong. Surely it must know what is right, and yet all it has the guts to do is sneak in a mini-budget so that the opposition does not have an opportunity to reply and respond. We cannot bring the budgetary measures before the appropriate committee for discussion and deliberation. What is wrong with this government which made all those promises to the Canadian public about what is good and what is not good? Unfortunately, the small business community cannot depend solely on the Small Businesses Loans Act and its tri-annual update.
The small business community cannot continue, as it were, to hang in, while governments in general ignore its basic needs on one hand, and swamp it with bureaucratic regulations, directives, controls, forms and general paper work on the other. The small firm sector is what the free enterprise system in this country was built on, and if we want this system as we know it to continue to exist, much more must be done in the way of the promotion and development of wide-ranging programs and policies.
I have said over and over again, in this House as well as outside it, that government must commit itself to developing an over-all policy, not just ad hoc amendments and legislation such as the legislation we are discussing today. This government must commit itself to an over-all policy to assist the small business community in dealing with a broad range of issues and concerns.
The party to which I belong has, on many occasions, put forward realistic recommendations for consideration by the government in dealing with this vital industrial sector and, again, we were in the process of implementing them. The hon. member for Capilano was in the process of implementing them when he was cut short. The Conservative government was cut short in trying to implement the many realistic programs and proposals which we had introduced and were in the process of introducing.
For example, here are just some of the programs which I personally have recommended in this House in the past, and 1 continued to do so: Give tax rebates and other incentives to those small businesses which invest in research and development, because incentive is the key word in small business. Yet under the Liberal administration of the past 12 years, incentive has virtually disappeared from the political vocabulary.
I turn to point two: to provide an incentive tax credit to any Canadian citizen who makes a direct investment in the equity of a Canadian-owned business. Again, we must give small business an incentive, and we must give Canadians the incentive not only to invest in small business but to keep their investment in Canadian small businesses. By such a program we would kill two birds with one stone-keep investment in
April 28, 1980

Canada, and support the small business sector at the same time.
Three: develop trade schools and apprenticeship programs. It is unfortunate that in a country like ours, in which there are now a million unemployed, we should be importing specialists and tradespeople instead of setting up expanded trade schools and apprenticeship programs here. We have to go abroad and bring in labour from other countries. It is a shame, when we have a million people unemployed, that we should have to depend on other countries for specialized labour. The Conservative government was in the process of developing more trade schools and apprenticeship programs when it was cut short by the Liberals and the New Democrats who do not have a program to replace the new programs we were recommending.
Point four: to establish a fixed proportion of government services and goods to be supplied by small business, in other words, a set-aside program. We have talked about this for years. Why should the majority of those called upon to produce products and services for the government be large corporations, many of them multinational corporations not Canadian-owned? Why cannot the government set aside part of its purchasing program strictly for Canadian small businesses which, more often than not, can provide products and services more effectively than the larger multinationals?
Five: exempt small businesses from the application of federal legislation potentially harmful to them. We often debate federal legislation which is geared to large businesses, forgetting what harmful effects many of these measures have on the small business sector, whether it is textile quotas, whether it is-

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext: The Bank Act.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
-or the Bank Act, as one of my hon. friends mentioned. There are many pieces of legislation dealt with in this House which are harmful to small business. The minister responsible for small businesses should take upon himself to make sure that small business is exempt from these provisions whenever they are harmful to that sector.
Six: develop, through incentives, a secondary manufacturing sector. Canada is the wealthiest country per capita in terms of natural resources, yet consider what happens: we dig up our natural resources, often using American or foreign firms, and sell those resources to West Germany, Japan and elsewhere, where they create productivity and employment. Then, very often, we buy back the finished product at inflated prices, though in many cases they were made out of natural resources which came from Canadian soil in the first place. Again, through incentives, we must begin to consider establishing a secondary manufacturing sector particularly within the small and medium-size business community which is the most capable when it comes to dealing with this aspect. As I say, we have an advantage because the natural resources are here as opposed to Japan or West Germany.
Governments in the past have closed their eyes to these possibilities. Their philosophy has been: just dig it out and ship
Small Businesses Loans Act
it abroad. If we had a secondary manufacturing sector here we would not be obliged to depend to the extent we do on the American economy when it comes to auto parts, for example.
One other point-and I shall be brief because I know my time is running out-calls for the total overhaul of the Federal Business Development Bank. From my point of view, its procedures are too cumbersome, too bureaucratic; there is too much red tape and too much security is demanded by way of collateral. I could tell you a dozen horror stories, Mr. Speaker. I recall when I was building up my own small business. At that time the Federal Business Development Bank was called the Industrial Development Bank. We needed expansion funds because our business was growing faster than we could get credit from the chartered banks. It took us six months to get the loan and four times the amount of collateral which we regarded as reasonable. I am sure if that bank had known my grandmother had gold fillings in her teeth, they would have asked for them, too! But I did not tell them. I might add that legal fees amounted to about 10 per cent of the total loan. Now, is that assistance to small business? The same kind of story is true today of the Federal Business Development Bank. That is not assistance to small business.
As I said earlier, bills such as the one before us are necessary for the sake of updating only. They do not constitute anything new or innovative. I believe the bill should have offered a lot more than it has, such as higher maximums, higher annual gross revenues for eligibility, an increase in the number of institutions offering the loans, the inclusion of working capital, and a far greater variety of reasons qualifying people for loans-not only those engaged in small business strictly defined but those engaged in the area of farming and fisheries as well.
I shall not dwell on this subject any longer because I anticipate putting forward these recommendations perhaps by way of amendment when the bill reaches committee stage. So, in closing, I should like to repeat what I have said often in this chamber, something which I believe is imperative if we are to preserve our democratic way of life.
If we wish the small business sector to continue and prosper in our society, as I am sure we all do-at least on the Liberal and Conservative sides; I am not so sure about those other clowns to my left-immediate action must be taken by the federal government to come up with an over-all, comprehensive program dealing with small business, rather than the present band-aid approach. I know the minister must be getting tired of hearing the phrase "band-aid approach" used so many times, but that is what it is and that is what has been applied for the last 12 years. The small business community is what the free enterprise system is all about. It is what this country was built on and what this country can prosper by.
Other countries, which are presently more fortunate than Canada with respect to unemployment, inflation, productivity and other benchmarks by which a standard of success is judged, have all concentrated their economic energies upon the small business sector. We still have a chance to keep the free enterprise system well and alive, building toward the future,

Small Businesses Loans Act
building on what we possess, building on the strength we have. But we must act at once before we lose this opportunity.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne had a great promise in it. It said something about an assurance that ceilings for loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act would be raised to $100,000. That, of course, was designed to sound good to the general unwashed. This is a ding-dong piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker. It is pure drivel. It does not mean anything with interest rates on prime at 16.75 per cent. And one over prime is 17.75 per cent-18 per cent. Well, my goodness gracious!
We are now going to increase the limit which the Government of Canada can guarantee to the big banks to $675 million from $600 million. Now, is that not an important piece of legislation for the big banks? Is that not wonderful for the big banks? The big banks will be happy about that. Also we will hear about the Bank Act later in this session. Is that not super? Are we not going to do something real fine for small business? We are going to give them money at one over prime, if they happen to qualify under the regulations in the act.
Let us look at the act and all the regulations required under it. Under section 7 of the act it is indicated that the governor in council may make regulations prescribing the forms, applications, reports and other documents required in connection with guaranteed loan improvements effective under the operations of the act. At one over prime we have got to go through the red tape, and at 18 points we still have to go through the red tape. This is to help small business. Is that not wonderful? How can one be the Minister of State for Small Businesses, (Mr. Lapointe) and expect to help small business by one more bit of regulation and red tape up to $100,000? This is providing that one's business does not have too much gross and providing that it comes under the regulations and the requirements of the minister. What is his regulatory power? It goes on a whole page and on to the next page right down to section (m) and the subsections. It goes on and on and on.
The poor small businessman coming up to apply for a loan will say to his banker, "Sir, I want a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act. I want to pay only one over prime." The banker is going to kick him out on his arse. This is what they call a help to small business. This is a real Liberal help to small business. They really want to help the small businessman. They want to give him all this advantage of paying one over prime. The guy could probably get the loan at one over prime without the red tape, and if he cannot, he will not get the loan anyway.
What are they going to guarantee with this one over prime loan? They are going to guarantee that the banks will get 90 per cent of their defaults covered. That is what they are talking about. They are talking about a piece of legislation which is so important that it was put into the Speech from the Throne. It was put in to help the unwashed who do not know
anything about small business to think that this government will do something for small business.
I see the minister walking out right now. 1 do not blame him for walking out. I would walk out too if I was the minister with this piece of legislation. This piece of legislation is a travesty on this Parliament. We were asked to debate urgent legislation. The Governor General in his imputations for this House said in the speech that we must rely on the good will of members and that we must get down to passing necessary legislation, the accumulation of essential legislation. This is called essential legislation; this is called legislation to help small business. I see the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) nodding his head. He thinks that this is great stuff. He has been so heavily involved in the small business field that he really knows what it is to earn a living and pay a payroll, as long as he is on the public service staff.
Let us get down to brass tacks. This is a bill which is just pure hokum to the general public. It has no intention of helping small business at all. It will not do a darned thing to help small business. It raises the limits the banks will receive. The big banks will receive the guarantee of the minister from $600 million to $675 million. It raises the size of the loan, providing the loan goes through all the regulatory processes, up to $100,000. I say, big deal, ding-dong legislation. It is a never mind bill. One cannot oppose the thing. It has got good intentions. It says something about small business. It is really intended to help. Maybe it will help the little guy a bit, but it will not do a darn thing for the business conditions of this country.
1 am disappointed that the minister has left because I would have liked to have asked him how many public servants are operating this wonderful piece of legislation, guiding the limits the banks will guarantee these loans? How many people does he have supervising the banks under the Small Businesses Loans Act? How many people are we paying as taxpayers of Canada to supervise these terribly difficult loans on which the poor small businessman only has to pay 18 per cent or 1.5 per cent a month? It is as easy as that. It is disgusting that the government should produce this legislation at all, that it should not come to the House of Commons with real concrete economic legislation dealing with the interest problems faced by business.
The other day I was doing some homework on the Bank Act.
I am glad the hon. member for Ottawa Centre is looking at me. While I was doing some homework on the Bank Act, I had some discussion with some bankers, and it appears to me that the banking system is taking the hide off business to pay for its mistakes by getting into the mortgage business and the consumer loans business. What they have to do to cover their hides and their losses with rising interest rates is to charge small business prime plus one over, plus two over or whatever, just to get enough income to cover the losses they are taking on their long-term mortgage portfolios, their long-term car finance portfolios, and their long-term chargex type portfolios which are guaranteed at rates of interest far below the current prime. The effect has been that the business community has
April 28, 1980

been diddled. Really, the minister should be talking about the Bank Act. He should be talking about how we will control interest factors charged to businesses that are productive and employment oriented in the country, rather than businesses which need the assistance of this act.
Frankly this act has never done anything for small business. This act started in 1961. Really, what has it done? What are the huge accomplishments? What are the enormous successes of a statute which has been cluttering up the books since 1961? What have they really accomplished with it? We could talk about the bureaucracy they have. We could talk about the number of people who are employed in the service of the Government of Canada as a result of this act. We could talk about the paperwork that has been organized. We could talk about the forms that have been prescribed under section 7. It goes on page after page. This is the kind of thing we get from a Liberal government. They have not got anything new to offer, so they keep on amending an old piece of legislation, and they do not justify this legislation by any tremendous assistance to small business. Yes, it sounds sexy if one wants to put it that way. It is great stuff, it will help small business. They are going to increase their loan limit to $100,000. That is not the kind of thing we should be doing in this Parliament.
Even though the Governor General, in speaking to us in the Speech from the Throne, was mouthing the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the people of Canada expect something out of this Parliament. They do not expect this kind of drivel. They expect something that is positive. They expect something that will inspire the entrepreneurial efforts of Canadians. What does this act do? It increases the loan limit to $100,000. It increases the guarantee limit to $675 million. That is all it does. At no time can we show in the administration of this act for nearly 20 years that it has really accomplished anything for small business, that it has really made it possible for small business to grow and develop, even though small business represents very close to half the employment in this country or more.
What has this act done? As a small businessman, would you bother going to your bank manager and saying, "Mr. Manager, you have got to put me under the Small Businesses Loans Act?" The truth of the matter is that you want the loan. If the manager says that it is 1.5 over prime, you will go for 1.5 over prime rather than upset the manager and try to beat him down to one over prime. That is what you are going to do. You are darned right you are going to do that. You are not going to say to Mr. Manager, "Fill out the forms under the Small Businesses Loans Act and get it for one over prime for me." Guess what! You are not going to get the loan at all if you play that kind of a game. You know it, I know it, and anybody who has been in business knows it.
This is cosmetic legislation designed for people who do not know any better. It is designed to put in a brochure so the government can say it has given something to small business. I suggest the government has done it to small business, not for
Small Businesses Loans Act
small business, and they have done it to the people of Canada, not for them.
The government has created a situation where it has gone to the public of Canada, and intends to go this year, to borrow $50 million every business day of the year. That is fresh money they require to pay for their wasteful expenditure programs. These are expenditure programs which they refuse to come to this country and the people of Canada and this House of Commons to say why they are required. The government requires $50 million fresh cash every business day.
Some small businessmen hold savings bonds. Some ordinary Canadians hold savings bonds, but $500 million in savings bonds have been cashed in the last three weeks.
What this government has done has driven up the price of capital. It has driven up the cost of interest in this country by excessive borrowing. If the government would even cut down its requirement to borrow by a couple of billion dollars, or the $3.7 billion the budget of December 11 would have allowed, there would have been more money on the market for businessmen to borrow. When there is more money around to borrow, the interest rate goes down. Businessmen are not concerned about whether they qualify under this piece of legislation. They are concerned about whether they can borrow money at a reasonable rate. What does this government do? It is going to do something great for the small businessman by increasing the amount of the ceiling to $100,000.
I guess our party will support this piece of nonsense. I guess we will send it to the committee. As the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek) says, I suppose we can make some amendments to it. However, you know it really is a ridiculous piece of nonsense. It does not do anything for people in small business. It does not help anybody. I bet you that the minister, if he were here, could not tell us one single person this piece of legislation has really helped. If you can get a loan you get the loan yourself. If you cannot get the loan then you do not get it.
Do you think a bank is going to give you a loan at one over prime when it thinks it can dig you for three over prime, just because you go to the manager and say, "Mr. Manager, did you not know there was a Small Businesses Loans Act? Did you not know that, Mr. Manager?" You know what the manager is going to say. He is going to say, "You do not qualify, buddy boy, because I ain't going to fill out the form." He will tell you to go down the street to the Bank of Nova Scotia. The Bank of Nova Scotia will tell you to go down the street to the Toronto-Dominion Bank. You can go all around the clock and eventually you might, if you do your politicking right, get somebody to fill out the forms, but then he will probably turn the whole thing down.
This is a lot of nonsense. Anybody who has been in business knows that. I see that the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley) knows that. He has been there before and he knows it is a lot of nonsense. It is a lot of nonsense; it is ding-dong legislation from a ding-dong government that does not know anything about business. The hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett)-

April 28, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act

speechtext:
She says she is sleeping. I do not think that even she expects there is very much in this legislation. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) was speaking about it and I do not think he believes there is very much in this legislation. This is a filler bill in order to keep people happy and let this government say it is doing something. The government can tell Mr. Bulloch it has done something for small business today. I hope Mr. Bulloch of the organization for small business appreciates that because he has really got something. He has got a wonderful bill. He has a really wonderful bill here. It is really going to make all his members rich and prosperous. It is going to help them all make a lot of money.
This is the kind of a bill that is really not worth the paper it is written on. You will not find a bank manager getting all worked up about this bill. They think it is great. They think, by golly, the Government of Canada has really come to the assistance of the little fellow. Here we have a bill that is supposed to help small business. Why does the government not have a bill before this House that says this government commits itself to buying the things it requires from small business? It should buy a percentage of government requirements in Canada from small business. It should buy a percentage of its stationery, paper clips, typewriters, and repair services from small business.
What about the things the government needs around this Hill and in its offices around the countryside? Is a percentage of that material purchased from small business? Are we going to hire no one except people from small businesses to do the typewriter repairs, fix up the adding machines and the computers in the manpower office in my city? Is that the kind of policy we have, or are we going to continue with a policy of only hiring the big boys, the powerful boys, and give the small businessmen this drivel in Bill C-17?
Bill C-17 represents the kind of nonsense that we get from this government. This is the kind of thing this government produces so that it can say it has done something. I can see all the press clippings now. They will indicate that in the month of April this government was able to pass through second reading so many pieces of legislation: Holy baldy! Holy baldy!
This ding-dong bill with its red tape, with its 17% per cent demand interest on the present rate will not do anything for the business people in the community. It is keeping us busy here tonight. We are having lots of fun. We can debate it back and forth, but the real problems of the small businessmen relate to the acquiring of equity capital. If this government really was intent on doing something it should produce some amendments to the Federal Business Development Bank Act in connection with the federal government making arrangements for equity capital for small business. The government should do something in respect of the Federal Business Development Bank taking less security and a little more risk on some of the development loan possibilities that exist in small business.
This bill really does not have much to offer. It limits the minister's liability to a bank. It is really a bill to guarantee a bank against a bum loan. In others words, if a bank has to make a loan, because of political pressure in a community, and it did not think it was a very good loan, that bank is protected by the government. As a matter of fact, if the banker felt he would probably lose he would probably fill out the necessary paperwork and make the loan. If it was a good loan the banker might even talk the client into taking the loan at 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent over prime because of the speed at which the loan would be processed. After all, if the interest rate at 1 per cent over prime is 17% per cent, or 18 per cent, and the rate at 2 per cent over prime is 18% per cent, what is the difference? At that level of prime, to a person who wants the money, the total interest factor on the improvement loan does not mean much. The important thing is how fast the loan can be approved and how quickly the man can get on with the job.
This bill really does not reduce interest rates at all. It really provides an assistance program for the big banks. That is what it is, it is the big bank improvement loan. We should call it the big bank improvement loan. We could say it is the Royal benefit plan, the Commercial benevolent plan, or the Montreal yes plan. That is really what it is.

If one really gets down to the matter, the only people who will file applications under this act are those whom the banks looks upon as people who cannot pay their bills anyway. The banks will try to stick the minister with a $100,000 liability. They can stick this minister with a lot of liabilities. He is a good fellow for liabilities. He is a liability to this government sometimes, and he must be a liability because he brought in this bill as a matter of urgent and pressing legislation. It is a bank benevolent act.
If a person really qualifies for the loan, then he will get the loan from his local bank. I can say, from my much experience in small business and arranging financing for small business through our banking system, that our banking system is very competent at organizing loans for small business. It does not want to be bothered with the red tape of this bill. In fact the banks will make these loans at 1 per cent over prime or not much more. The banks will make these loans in some cases with minimal security if the credit worthiness of the borrower is there. It is only if the credit worthiness is not there or if the person cannot or will not pay, that the bank will attempt to stick the minister with the loan.
The minister will end up with a bank bureaucracy to look after the situations where the bank has ended up sticking it to him. This bill is very typical of Liberal legislation in that it is designed to increase the size of the bureaucracy and designed to be colour-coated to make a good impression. As far as business is concerned, as far as the guy on the street who is running a small manufacturing business, a store, or something in the construction field, is concerned, this is a bunch of nonsense. If such a person goes to his banker tomorrow and says, "Bill C-17 has been passed and you have to give me a
April 28, 1980

loan of $100,000, cheapie, cheapie, cheap", he will get the cold shoulder from his banker. You and 1 know that, Mr. Speaker, and the minister ought to know it as well.
The minister has been involved in small business enough to know that this piece of legislation is purely cosmetic or drivel legislation, the kind of useless bill that really does not accomplish very much and that is only there to paint the picture that this government is doing something for small business. This government has "bureaucratitus". It is a disease. The government passes legislation that provides for regulation, and I mentioned earlier the regulations in section 7, and I can go on through three-quarters of this bill about regulations.
Obviously, this is a bill that is designed to employ people. It gives the minister more people to work for him, more people in the civil service, more people to regulate and more forms to produce. It is probably good for the printing industry, and if the minister were really enthusiastic about the bill, he would organize the printing of the business forms required for this legislation so that the work would go to companies defined under the legislation as being small businesses.
This legislation will not do very much for small business. I will support the bill, but 1 really do not know why it was introduced as part of a program of a government that purports to do something for people, that purports to create, that purports to produce, and that purports to be interested in the affairs of Canada. After the government increases the deficit to $14 billion and brings in a requirement to borrow $11.75 billion on the capital markets of the country which will drive interest rates up and make things difficult for business, it proceeds to come along with this piece of camouflage, this piece of ding dong, this piece of nothingness and say that small business loans will receive favourable treatment.
The minister knows that it is nonsense, and anybody who has been in small business knows it as well. This bill is cosmetic and has no value in the total picture of the business community in Canada. This is typical of the kind of bill which this government produces. It is unfortunate that we on this side must support or, to some extent, go along with such a measure simply because there may be some conceivable benefit. So, I believe that we must conceivably go along.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the best suggestion that could be given to the government today as it addresses the problem of what it might be able to do to assist small business is that it try, through some magic that is not obvious in this piece of legislation, to put itself in the place of a small businessman. I suggest that Bill C-19 refuses to address the problem that the small businessman is facing today.
I think back to 1977 when I entered federal politics and to what the then prime minister of Canada said, that he would like to wrestle inflation to the ground. He gave the people of Canada a commitment in that year by forecasting that inflation would not exceed 4 per cent. He followed that forecast with an apology by blaming the pressures of inflation on the Canadian economy on other countries. In 1978 he said, "We will hold inflation in Canada to no more than 6 per cent." In
Small Businesses Loans Act
fact, what has happened is far from the promises which the Prime Minister gave. His promises are not inconsistent with the promises his party made during the most recent election campaign.
I am sure that the business community in Canada was looking to this new government which took office only a short time ago for some injections into the economy that would help small businessmen. As a small businessman for some 25 years, I can say that this piece of legislation offers absolutely nothing new over what has occurred in the past decade, which was a complete disregard for the small businessman as he faced the pressures of inflation. We all know what members opposite thought of the "Diefenbuck", the 97-cent dollar, and we all know that when a piece of legislation is introduced in the House that offers some positive measures with regard to the fact that the small businessman must get better value for his dollar, he must also get better value from the government.
This piece of legislation, Bill C-17, will not correct what in fact is actually happening. What is happening to the business community in Canada today is that investments are leaving the country. No one wishes to invest in small business because of the bad treatment it gets from government. The government is supposed to set an example, and introduce legislation to prove it. What the government is doing in this bill is saying it would like to see the banks guaranteed for their losses incurred through the higher frequencies of bankruptcies in Canada today. This way the banks will lend to small business.
Small business is a bad risk because small business cannot get good value for its dollars spent. And why can small business not get good value for its dollars spent? It is because of the devalued dollar, the waste in government, and the high inflation rate, which was forecast in 1977 by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to be 4 per cent. Then it went to 6 per cent, 8 per cent, and 10 per cent. I say to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe), why can the government not introduce legislation that honestly tries to help the business community? Why do they dress up legislation and have headlines in the newspapers to the effect that the Small Businesses Loans Act is coming in when all it is in reality is a means for the banks to guarantee 90 per cent of their risk capital to an already bankrupt industry, small business, for job creation and employment?
Today the small business sector provides more than half of the total employment in Canada. We have a tremendously high unemployment rate. It approaches one million or more, if the figures were accurate. It actually exceeds one million because it eliminates those people who no longer qualify because of the effect of Liberal policies on the UIC qualifications.
This government is totally responsible for the giant octopus approach to the economy. The government is reaching out with its tentacles and is sucking like a giant octopus every nickel and every penny out of the small business community until there is nothing left for that octopus known as the government

April 28, 1980
Small Businesses Loans Act
to live on. It grows with its own greed and the person mainly affected is the small businessman.
How nice it would have been if the government had honoured some of the commitments it had made to the business community in Canada. How long can this giant cookie monster keep reaching into the cookie jar sucking every ounce of blood out of the business community until it has created the threat of unemployment for 50 per cent of the potential work force in Canada today?
If they do not smarten up soon, and introduce small business legislation that addresses the principal problem in business today-if they do not soon face the fact that the business community is going bankrupt with them, may 1 remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the spending of this government at some $60 billion represents 30 per cent more than they expect to take in? What business in Canada today could remain operative when spending 25 per cent more than it earns-sucking out of the people of Canada $1 out of every $4 they pay in taxes in order to satisfy their own greed?
The government's greed is nothing more than an insatiable search for power. They will tell the people of Canada anything, lead them down the garden path to nowhere, and in reality what the people get is nothing. This piece of legislation offers nothing new-no new outlook, no new approach or new direction for the running of this country.
When 1 ran for election in 1977 it was because I was finding it increasingly difficult to stay in business because of the greed of government and bureaucracy with its paper work. Why can the government not look at small business and design a very basic piece of legislation and give some credibility to the Minister of State for Small Businesses? It is not fair to shove him in some back room office and tell him that it is his responsibility to solve the problems of the country while, at the same time, giving him no teeth with which to attack the problem. If the minister is sincere-and I am sure he is-in wanting to help the small business community, he should introduce legislation that would cut bureaucracy, that would reduce the 60 per cent inefficiency in the civil service, that would offer funds to small businessmen at an interest rate they could afford. Why doesn't he do these things instead of introducing a meaningless piece of legislation?
This bill does nothing more than say to the business people of Canada today, "We are going to guarantee your loan to the bank; we are going to make sure that those big corporate giants known as the banks and trust companies are not going to lose any more on that problem that we, as a government, created, so we are going to insure the banks against losses in business."
When I approached the Industrial Development Bank in 1971, in 1972, and in 1974, Mr. Speaker, I found it increasingly difficult to obtain a loan. The banks are not interested, and this legislation does not offer the incentive for the bank or the lending institution to help the small businessman.
The government does not offer business people any incentive to run their businesses effectively, efficiently, economically
and practically. The government cannot run its own house, so how does it expect the business community to pay any attention to a piece of legislation which does nothing more than guarantee the loan to the bank-90 per cent and write off 10? The banks can write off 10 per cent at the exorbitant interest rate of 18 per cent that our government is proposing to charge them.
I think this bill is a piece of rubbish, Mr. Speaker. The problem of the business community is totally ignored. There are not enough businessmen on the other side of the House to design a piece of legislation that will be helpful to that community.
What is a small businessman with a demand loan at the bank at up to 20 per cent interest, depending on the risk, a private loan from an individual paying up to 22 per cent, another loan from a mother or father paying dear knows what they can afford to pay, going to do with this legislation? Absolutely nothing, Mr. Speaker. He cannot consolidate his loans, nor can he make himself solvent because the legislation will not allow the small businessman to obtain working capital. The major problem in the business community today is not building a business or buying an expensive piece of equipment; it is staying in business. How can people stay in business with this kind of legislation? How can the small businessman become solvent again through the pressures of high interest rates when the government ignores him, when the government cannot even set the example for the business community to follow?
The real responsibility of the government today is to create a climate for small business, and not to meddle in the market place, not create the paperwork, not put the burden on the businessman to fill in reports and account to everybody for everything he or she does. A business is run best when the government stays out of the marketplace. What the government is doing with this piece of garbage is entering the market place with a bill which is mountainous in scope, as one of my colleagues said, and which is not even comprehensible to the average businessman. He wants something simple-for the government to make funds available to the business community in order that people can obtain working capital, can consolidate debts, can get their cash flow in line with income.
The government is taking more from the small businessman than he can afford to pay. You are taking $1 out of every $4 in taxes paid today. You, as a government, are responsible. You are taking from business people in Canada today more than they can afford to pay.
I suggest that two things should be in this act in order to enable the business community to survive. The first one is for the government to set an example and to live by the Auditor General's report which shows the government is a bad manager. There should be people in control of government who will address this major problem of how to run their own house, how to run Parliament, how to run the country.
You cannot do it. You did not do it for 12, 13, 14 or 17 years, and all of a sudden you are back in office. That is not because you have a new program. You do not. That is why you
April 28, 1980

are sitting on the opposite side of the House. We had a program and you did not, but we did not have a chance to turn the train around. You got the train running downhill in Canada for 17 years. We did not have a chance to get that second track going out west in order that we could bring it back.
I say to the government, if you do not get your ship in order, if you do not address the problem facing the business community today, and quickly-I see both businessmen on the other side are laughing-I say if they do not address the problem quickly there will not be any business community left in Canada to save.
Do you realize that you, responsible people as you are, responsible people as you should be, are currently-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, do hon. members on the other side of the House who are reported to be creditable, sincere people, realize that this country cannot go on spending almost 50 cents of every dollar compared to the United States which spends as low as 23 cents? There are just not enough dollars to sustain that kind of octopus. The government has to get its hand out of the cookie jar. It has to remove the paperwork that is the burden on the small business community. The government has to cut that spending program from $60 billion to what it has to spend. This government must set an example for the business community, an example which the business community can look up to, not look down at.
As long as this government continues as a government, and as long as we allow it to spend 25 per cent or 30 per cent more than it takes in each year, the government will go the route of the business community, that is, it will go down the drain. When the government goes down the drain, we all lose. That is exactly the course the train is on now. We are going down the drain. The government is refusing to face the facts, it is refusing to address the problems of the business community and refusing to make working capital available to the small businessman so he can consolidate his debts. I say 18 per cent interest will not do it. The business community cannot survive on this program. The government ignores it. The government offers a program that is only of benefit to the major banking institutions.
We are at a time now in history when the people of Canada must be conservative. The people of Canada must learn to spend less. When I say the people of Canada, I say that the government will have to start living within its means if any legislation, particularly if a piece of legislation to be credibly studied in this House, addressing the problem of the business community is to be given any credibility at all. Having said that, with a little bit of restraint now shown by government- and it is not in its Minnie Mouse budget-we could perhaps slow up the train. But we must keep the business community shovelling the coal in. We must generate that 50 per cent of
Small Businesses Loans Act
the work force that the business community generates. We will not do it by strangling these people with increased paperwork and bills like this which are of no assistance to them whatsoever.
We all know about the disasters in the post office and how well the Government of Canada runs anything that it sticks its hand into. We say: less government intervention, more responsibility given to business, less requirements of business to account to government, and the net result will be a reduction in our deficit, an improvement in the business community, and credibility to this government which it sorely needs.
What we need is a more businesslike approach from members opposite. We should not be continually laughing at the small business community. When we do that, we discredit ourselves. We have to give importance to the need to assist them and not give them lip service. We have to stop the intrusion of a government in the economy. We have to stop large bureaucracies draining life out of the business community. We have to bring in legislation that honestly and sincerely addresses the problem, and not give some front page headline story to this bill that it is going to offer the saving salvation for the business community when, in reality, it is going to do nothing of the sort.
A small businessman going broke today is not going broke because he cannot borrow $100,000. He is going broke because he cannot borrow $5,000. He cannot get enough money to meet his payroll. He cannot make the payments to the CIP, to the government. He cannot meet the payroll to his spouse, so the deduction that the government proposes to give to the spouses in small business, to a large number of businesses in Canada today will not mean a thing. He is not paying any income tax. He is not paying any money to the government. Consequently, we do not have enough dollars to run our own House here. Let us get our House expenses down. We have to move away from leaning toward the free handouts that is pressured on us by members to my left.
We have to stop realizing that every time there is a need in the country we look to the government to pick up the tab. Every time you do that, you strangle small business. Every time one gives in to a pressure group, any time one makes an election promise-and members opposite make election promises that will cost money-the business community is strangled with excesses of spending far in excess of revenue.
Let us try to put the country back on its feet. Let us do everything we can to be a good example to the business community in Canada. Let us consider, just for a moment, the possibility of getting off the back of the small businessman. Let us take a moment to think of what a saving it would be to a small businessman with a staff of two or three if he did not have to devote 30 per cent, 40 per cent or 50 per cent of his time to filling out papers in order to satisfy the bureaucrats that the system that we have implemented, here with all of our legal advice, is the best system for that small businessman. In reality, our major problem in Canada today, whether it is the labour unions, small business, or in government, is productivity or the lack of it. We cannot improve productivity in the small

April 28, 1980
Adjournment Debate
business community if we do not get off the backs of these people, or say, and mean what you say, that we will cut the paperwork and set up systems within ministries today, not a new ministry or a new portfolio with 125 administering it, but systems within the existing ministries in that front bench across the way whereby their own ministerial expenses will be cut. And at the same time perhaps they will be able to cut the paperwork that is putting a burden on the small businessman. If hon. members opposite do not address these subjects soon, they can expect the kinds of problems that are compounding as they continue.
I remind hon. members opposite that in the first quarter of 1979 there were 1,465 bankruptcies. In September, 1979, there were over 2,000 bankruptcies. I would also like to remind hon. members opposite that our percentage based on the number of businesses in Canada, of bankruptcies, is not very commendable when one looks at the situation to the south of us. We have a lot to do to put our ship in order, in order that we can even compare half favourably to other free enterprise countries. The main problem is the drain that the members opposite, the ministers, and the minister for small business are ignoring-the drain on the pocketbooks of the small businessmen.
1 plead with the minister for small business in his wisdom to bring in a good, honest piece of legislation that will say to the business community of Canada, "We do care and we will reduce government expenses. We will cut the inflation rate," not big insignificant promises of inflation rates of 4 per cent, 6 per cent or 8 per cent when in reality we have double digit inflation.
Let us look at what the Prime Minister has referred to as perhaps a new fresh outlook, and involve Canadians in that process of bringing credibility to government and success to small business.

subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-REQUEST FOR PARLIAMENTARY DEBATE BEFORE SYSTEM PUT INTO FULL EFFECT
METRIC CONVERSION-REQUEST FOR PARLIAMENTARY DEBATE BEFORE SYSTEM PUT INTO FULL EFFECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the result of some questions asked on metric conversion as it would pertain to the imposing of forced implementation of metric conversion on some six million or eight million people in Canada on January 1, whether they want it or not, I asked a question in the House of Commons on April 23. I addressed the question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In his absence, I referred it to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). He was reluctant to answer it and passed it on to the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe).
The question dealt with two matters. I felt that the Government of Canada, against the will of the people of Canada, and without due process or consultation, had forced metric conversion on the Canadian people, in particular the cities of Peterborough, Kamloops and Sherbrooke. I asked the minister for small businesses if he would consider bringing into the House an act to be debated which would afford the opportunity for the citizens of Canada, Jo have their input into this legislation which will bring metric conversion into retail stores, and the meat stores in particular.
The minister responded that he was under the impression that metric conversion had been debated in the House in 1971. On April 25, last Friday, the minister for small businesses stated that he recognized that he was in error. He said, "I recognize quite humbly that there has been no legislation on metrication that was passed as such."
With that in mind, I would like to advise this government that the contrast between the United States method of handling the implementation of metric conversion in the retail stores versus Canada's method, is the same as looking at a democracy and looking at a dictatorship. What has happened in Canada is without the due process of parliamentary debate and the citizens of Canada being given the opportunity to choose. The Government of Canada, in its lack of wisdom, elected through orders in council or ministerial direction to force metrication last year on three test centres in Canada. The results were disastrous. The response against the program was overwhelming. In light of this, and in light of the adverse reaction to this forced metric conversion without debate, 1 look forward very optimistically to the minister's statement in the House.
On April 23 the Minister of State for Small Businesses, when 1 asked whether he would allow full parliamentary discussion on metric conversion, responded "that it would be exam-
April 28, 1980

ined". I pursued the question with a supplementary and asked whether he would introduce a bill. Again he said he would review the suggestion. In light of the throne speech of the Prime Minister and the government, in which they assured the people of Canada that they would take into consideration the wishes of the people as they proceeded with running this country, 1 sincerely hope they will avail themselves of the opportunity to introduce legislation before they implement metric in 21 cities in Canada on January 1, 1981.
I remind this House than when metric is imposed without the due process of debate on January 1, 1981, approximately six million Canadians will be affected over the next year. If the government refuses to introduce legislation in this House, it will be taking a very hard-handed and dictatorial approach to what we all ran for office to do, that is, represent the majority wishes of our constituents in Canada.
Perhaps some hon. members opposite would like to know that they are going to get metric in St. John's, Dartmouth-Halifax, Quebec City, Montreal, Ottawa-Hull, Hamilton, Brantford, Windsor, Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge, Victoria, Nanaimo, and on the list goes. I would like hon. members opposite to realize that in April of 1981 they are going to have it in Charlottetown, Moncton, Fredericton, back in Montreal for a second phase, Mississauga, Toronto, Scarborough, Kingston, Oshawa and St. Catharines. There is something in this long list I would like to draw to the attention of this House. They have left Peterborough off the list.
Peterborough went into forced metric conversion in 1979. It has presented, through delegations to this government, the adverse effects it felt. My quarrel is not with the metric system per se but with the way it is being introduced. In last Saturday's edition of the Ottawa Citizen an article dealing with the report of the metric overview board includes the following quotation from that report:
The majority of Canadians are not prepared to accept metric conversion, despite active promotion of metric by the Metric Commission over an extended period. Many people also view the metrication program to be costly-
Another hindrance for small business.
-inconvenient and confusing, having few if any practical benefits.
A preliminary report by the overview committee last November listed more examples of public opposition to the implementation of metric, but truly to understand the nature of the opposition, it is probably best to go to the people who were the guinea pigs, the people of the city of Peterborough.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State, Small Businesses):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-REQUEST FOR PARLIAMENTARY DEBATE BEFORE SYSTEM PUT INTO FULL EFFECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has not yet decided on a date to proceed with the implementation of the retail scales metric conversion program.
The previous government imposed a postponement of a minimum of one year on the continuation of scales conversion across the country. The weights and measures regulations setting conversion dates for the different areas covering the country were rescinded on February 19, 1980, but the provision for weighing and selling in metric still remains. In the three pilot areas almost all the food stores in Sherbrooke still retail in metric; in Kamloops about half of the stores switched
Adjournment Debate
back to pounds; and in Peterborough almost all stores are back to pounds.
The national co-ordinating body which planned this conversion is the working group on scales in the retail food industry. This body met on March 24 of this year and indicated the majority of the retail representation in the working group are prepared to recommend a start of scale conversion on January 1, 1981, provided that this receives the support of government regulation over the entire industry, and with a positive public attitude toward conversion created by that time.
The working group further gave its chairman a mandate to make the government aware of its concerns and, if its recommendations receive the approval and support of government, to recall the working group to implement a program of scale conversion covering the two-year period starting January 1, 1981.
The working group on scales is composed of representatives from the retail food and scales industries, and from consumers' groups. Associations represented include the Canadian Federation of Retail Grocers, the Retail Council of Canada, the Retail Merchants Association of Canada, and the Consumers' Association of Canada.
Note that weights and measures in Canada have been regulated under the Weights and Measures Act, through the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The working group on scales responded to the view of food retailers and consumers that retail food scale conversion be supported by legislation in order to ensure an orderly conversion and fair and uniform advertising practices. The working group now recommends that the proposed new schedules should also be supported by regulations and by a reinforced promotional campaign.
Our review will consider the views of all the interested parties involved in the conversion of scales in the retail food industry.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-WINNIPEG-RAIL RELOCATION-SUGGESTED REVERSAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-WINNIPEG-RAIL RELOCATION-SUGGESTED REVERSAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in February of 1979 I raised a question in the House in regard to the federal government, the Liberal government of the day, making up its mind one way or another as to whether it would provide funds for CP rail relocation in Winnipeg. After much procrastination they decided they would have another study. Well, we have just received the results of that study within the last couple of weeks and they show it would cost something like $168 million for rail relocation in Winnipeg.
As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) pointed out to me last week, however, there are no funds available for rail relocation. I do not understand why Liberal governments are continually asking for studies on rail relocation in Winnipeg when they do not have any funds for rail relocation. What kind

April 28, 1980
Adjournment Debate
of game are they playing with the people of Winnipeg? Tonight we have the parliamentary secretary answering for the Minister of Transport. Tie is calling for more studies. And the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) wants more studies too. They all want more studies, but they are not prepared to put up one red cent for rail relocation. This is absolutely ludicrous in light of the statements we heard from the right hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau) when he was prime minister in 1979. Rail relocation, he said then, was the Liberal approach. Well, if it is the Liberal approach, let them put up the funds.
Under the rail relocation formula 50 per cent comes from the federal government and the remaining 50 per cent is split equally between the provincial and municipal governments. If Ottawa is not prepared to put up something between $85 million and $100 million, then let them stop all these studies and this silly nonsense about wanting more studies about rail relocation. Let them put their money where their mouth is. The Minister of Transport told me the other day that the door is not closed, that there might possibly be DREE funds available. 1 hope the parliamentary secretary has some kind of announcement to make tonight about DREE funds, and I hope it is not $3 million or $4 million. If he cannot stand up tonight and tell us it is $85 million to $100 million, it will be further evidence they are leading us down the garden path.
There is another point 1 want to make clear tonight. This deliberate delay with regard to building the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass, because the Liberal government will not provide funding for the CP rail relocation, will cost Winnipeg an additional $2.8 million in construction fees, and I want a commitment from the parliamentary secretary that Ottawa will reimburse the city for the cost of this delay in providing funds while studies, studies, and yet more studies were being held. They will have to pay the additional $2.8 million which the city of Winnipeg will have to raise due to the 14-month delay in building the overpass.
The Minister of Transport stated to me the other day that everybody and his aunt want rail relocation. Well, not everybody and his aunt have been asking for it. It is the Minister of Transport, the former minister of transport, the present Minister of Employment and Immigration, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael), and the Prime Minister who have been asking for more and more studies. So, the onus is on the present Liberal government to provide some kind of funding to the tune of $85 million to $ 100 million.
Rail relocation has to be initiated by federal legislation and federal funding. They are committed to making a firm commitment to produce $85 million to $100 million in funds. Then the provincial government will be put on the spot to see what they will come up with. The Minister of Transport was critical the other day because he said that the Manitoba government has not said much about providing funding for rail relocation. But the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba cannot make any firm commitment for funds until the senior government makes a firm commitment because it is their legislation.
We have heard the statements from the previous minister of federal-provincial affairs. Lie gave tips to the city of Winnipeg on how to obtain funds for rail relocation, and he was so concerned about the grain handling problems in Winnipeg, that they are a major concern of the federal government, and the possible relocation of yards. He went on and on about the backup of grain cars. He was concerned about grain cars and grain movement, but when the final crunch comes, they do not have any money to put up at all. All we have is the UTAP funds which the province of Manitoba is prepared to turn over to the city, $7.2 million of the $10 million which was allotted to the province, but that is the only funding they have. The city of Winnipeg and the province do not have a bottomless pit of money to bring forward for CP rail relocation.
I hope the parliamentary secretary tonight has a firm commitment to give us. I hope he will announce that he has found $85 million to $100 million in DREE, or if they cannot come up with the funds, for heaven's sake say that you are going to forget about rail relocation and will grant a permit to build the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. Everybody would like to see the rail relocation go through, but if they cannot come up with the funding, then we will have to go with the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass.
I want to remind the parliamentary secretary that the two bridges crossing the tracks now are under weight restrictions. 1 hope the Liberal government is not waiting for these bridges to be closed permanently and then maybe come up with some solution. We cannot go on and on with this procrastination, stalling, and calling for more and more studies. I hope the parliamentary secretary will stand on his feet tonight and give us a firm commitment one way or the other.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-WINNIPEG-RAIL RELOCATION-SUGGESTED REVERSAL OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the conclusion of the railway relocation study in Winnipeg, I have been involved in reviewing the study and have conferred with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and Transport Canada officials about the study findings. In this process both the minister and myself have used the consultative approach. For instance, on April 24 the minister met with representatives of the city and the province to exchange views on the course of action to follow.
1 am sure everyone here will agree that removing the railway tracks from the downtown of cities is a very desirable action. The cost of doing so, however, may in many cases be prohibitive. In the case of Winnipeg, the minister has already indicated in the House earlier that Transport Canada does not have funds, other than those available under the urban transportation assistance program, to allocate to Winnipeg. During the meeting on April 24 he reiterated his position on that subject in light of the report that the estimated net cost for relocation of the yard is $128 million, and $169 million is the estimated net cost for moving the yard and its main line.
April 28, 1980

I would note that the city is likely to construct the Sher-brook-McGregor arterial roadway system even if the rail lines are removed from their present location.
The study which was undertaken by the federal government was carried out because the city provided no estimate on the cost of relocation when they applied to build the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass.
Before the meeting with the representatives of the city and the province adjourned, the minister agreed to approach the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to find out whether this department has funds that might be allocated to the relocation project in Winnipeg. This possibility is being
Adjournment Debate
explored expeditiously so that an early decision can be reached.
I doubt very much that even should the federal government be in a position to increase its own financial commitment proportionately, the province and the city in turn would be willing to give the proposed CPR rail relocation in Winnipeg their corresponding priorized financial participation. Such an essential component of their co-operative involvement can only be resolved through jointly held negotiations.
